what_its_for: This is a combination birth control pill that prevents pregnancy. It contains two hormones — a progestin (norgestrel) and an estrogen (ethinyl estradiol) — that work together to stop your body from releasing an egg, thicken the mucus in your cervix so sperm cannot reach an egg, and change the lining of your uterus. When taken correctly, it is over 99% effective at preventing pregnancy.
how_to_take: Take one pill by mouth every day at the same time each day. Pick a time that is easy to remember, such as with breakfast or at bedtime. Swallow the pill whole with a glass of water. You can take it with or without food. If it upsets your stomach, try taking it with a meal or snack. Follow the pills in order on the pack — do not skip pills or take them out of order. Your pack may contain 21 active pills or 28 pills (21 active pills plus 7 reminder pills). If you have a 28-day pack, take the reminder pills at the end to keep your daily habit going. You will likely get your period during the reminder pill week.
dosing: Take one pill every day for 21 or 28 days depending on your pack type. For a 21-day pack: take one pill daily for 21 days, then stop for 7 days, then start a new pack. For a 28-day pack: take one pill every day without stopping, then start a new pack the next day. Your doctor will tell you when to start your first pack — usually on the first day of your period or on the first Sunday after your period begins. If you start on any day other than day 1 of your period, use a backup method of birth control (like condoms) for the first 7 days.
missed_dose: If you miss 1 pill: Take it as soon as you remember, even if that means taking 2 pills in one day. Then continue your regular schedule. You probably do not need a backup method. If you miss 2 pills in a row in week 1 or 2: Take 2 pills the day you remember and 2 pills the next day, then continue as usual. Use condoms or another backup method for 7 days. If you miss 2 pills in a row in week 3, or miss 3 or more pills at any time: Throw away the rest of the pack and start a new pack the same day if you are a Day 1 starter, or wait until Sunday to start a new pack if you are a Sunday starter. Use backup birth control for 7 days. You may not have a period that month, which is normal. If you miss your period two months in a row, call your doctor to rule out pregnancy. When in doubt about missed pills, use a backup method and call your pharmacist or doctor.
storage: Store at room temperature between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep the pills away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store in the bathroom where it can get hot and steamy. Keep the pill pack in its original packaging. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. Do not use pills past the expiration date printed on the pack. Dispose of unused or expired pills safely — ask your pharmacist about a medication take-back program near you.
what_to_avoid: Avoid smoking — especially if you are over 35 years old. Smoking while taking this pill greatly increases your risk of serious blood clots, stroke, and heart attack. Try to quit smoking before or while using this medication. Avoid taking this pill if you are pregnant or think you might be pregnant. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice in large amounts, as it may affect how this medication works. Avoid taking St. John's Wort (an herbal supplement), as it can make the pill less effective. Some medications can make birth control pills less effective, including certain antibiotics (like rifampin), seizure medications, and HIV medications — always tell every doctor and pharmacist that you are on birth control. Avoid prolonged bed rest or sitting still for long periods (like long flights) without moving around, as birth control pills can increase the risk of blood clots.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you notice any of these warning signs — think 'ACHES': Abdominal pain (severe stomach pain), Chest pain or shortness of breath, Headache that is severe or unusual, Eye problems such as blurry or loss of vision, Severe leg pain or swelling (especially in the calf). Also call your doctor if you have: yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), unusual or heavy vaginal bleeding, a lump in your breast, signs of a severe allergic reaction (rash, hives, trouble breathing, swelling of your face or throat), depression or mood changes, or if you miss two periods in a row. Tell your doctor about all medications and supplements you take, as many can interact with birth control pills.
when_it_works: If you start on the first day of your period, the pill works right away to prevent pregnancy. If you start on any other day, use a backup method of birth control for the first 7 days. It may take a few months for your periods to become regular and for side effects like spotting or nausea to go away. The pill does NOT protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs) — use condoms to protect against STIs.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Do not use this medication if you are pregnant. If you become pregnant while taking this pill, stop taking it right away and call your doctor. Breastfeeding: This medication is generally not recommended while breastfeeding because it can reduce your milk supply. Talk to your doctor about progestin-only pills or other contraception options while nursing. Teenagers: This medication is safe and effective for teenagers who have already started their periods. Older adults (over 35): If you are over 35 and smoke, you should NOT use this medication due to a high risk of heart attack, stroke, and blood clots. Speak to your doctor about other birth control options. Liver disease: Do not use this medication if you have liver disease or liver tumors. People with migraines with aura: Talk to your doctor before using this pill, as it may increase the risk of stroke. People with diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, or a family history of blood clots should discuss the risks carefully with their doctor before starting this medication.
